Research Bits: Aug. 10

Shares

Thin chip stacking; analog CAM with MoS2; sensor-level processing and memory.

August 10th, 2026 -

By: Jesse Allen

Thin chip stacking
Researchers from Pohang University of Science & Technology (POSTECH), Korea Institute of Industrial Technology (KITECH), and Texas A&M University developed a process that simultaneously transfers chips and forms interconnects, enabling them to reliably stack ten chips, each about 14μm thick.
The process combines transfer printing for precision placement and in-situ bonding to form metallic bonds during chip transfer in low-temperature and low-pressure conditions.  Interlayer alignment errors remained extremely small even after repeated stacking, and structural warpage was significantly suppressed.
“We achieved an integration density approximately four times higher than existing HBM technologies,” said Seok Kim, a professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at POSTECH, in a statement. “We expect this technology to become a key enabling technology for future high-performance AI semiconductors and next-generation memory systems.” [1]
Analog CAM with MoS2
Researchers from the University of Hong Kong, Fudan University, and National University of Singapore designed an analog content-addressable memory (CAM) utilizing 2D molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) flash memories with antimony as the contact electrode.
The CAM requires only two transistors per cell, enabling it to directly process continuous analog signals. The fabricated 8 × 16 CAM array with 256 MoS2 flash memory devices demonstrated a high read-out current of over 60 μA μm−1 and an ON/OFF ratio exceeding 109, with energy consumption of under 0.1 femtojoules per search per cell and a latency of 36 picoseconds. It was able to calculate the analog Hamming distance for machine learning classification approximately 108 times faster than a standard CPU.
“From an application perspective, search operations are incredibly valuable,” explained Professor Li. “The ‘attention mechanism’ that serves as the foundation for Large Language Models (LLMs) is essentially a search process—retrieving information from a compressed knowledge base. We are exploring how to use this high-performance hardware to implement search mechanisms for large AI models,” said Can Li, associate professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the Faculty of Engineering at HKU, in a press release.
“Tasks like smartphone facial recognition could be completed instantly on the device without uploading private data to the cloud. While large-scale commercialization still requires overcoming engineering challenges in packaging, this research has successfully proven the principle, providing a clear blueprint for next-generation, high-performance AI hardware.” [2]
Sensor-level processing and memory
Researchers from Oregon State University built an optoelectronic device that integrates light sensing, memory, and signal processing in a single phototransistor.
The device is constructed from an oxide semiconductor, which serves as the transistor channel that carries electrical current, while an organic photosensitive material on top absorbs light and generates electrical charges. When charges become trapped within the photosensitive layer, they continue to influence the current flowing through the oxide semiconductor even after the light is removed, allowing the device to retain a memory of past optical signals.
“Our optoelectronic device introduces a new hardware capability that may enable more efficient processing of information directly at the sensor level,” said Larry Cheng, professor of electrical engineering and computer science at OSU, in a press release. “Unlike conventional memory that is designed to preserve information, our device can electronically control how memories strengthen or decay.”
The position of the trapped charges relative to the transistor channel can be changed by applying an electrical gate voltage. Moving the charges closer to the transistor channel strengthens their electrical influence and prolongs the memory effect, while moving them farther away weakens it and speeds the loss of stored charges, causing the memory to fade.
“This light-sensitive memory with a programmable memory lifetime creates a tunable time window for processing visual and other sensor signals directly where they are detected, a capability that could enable more efficient vision systems and other sensor-based AI technologies,” Cheng added. [3]
References
[1] U. Kim, J. Kim, S. Jeong, et al. Transfer printing and in-situ bonding for ultra-high-density integration. Results in Engineering. Volume 3, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rineng.2026.111194
[2] G. Gao, B. Wen, N. Yang, et al. Sb-contacted MoS2 flash memory for analogue in-memory searches. Nat. Nanotechnol. 21, 198–206 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-025-02089-7
[3] A. Ullah, R. Lamug, T. Sarker, et al. Neuromodulator-Inspired Gate-Tunable Tetracene–Metal Oxide Phototransistor for Adaptive Optoelectronic Memory and Neuromorphic Computing. Advanced Functional Materials 36, no. 56 (2026): e75942. https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.75942
